newsitem.title: UK: C&W hangs up on Germany's Veba.
newsitem.headline: C&W hangs up on Germany's Veba.

text.p: Britain's Cable and Wireless (C&W) hung up on its German partner on Friday, the latest alliance to break up as phone giants jostle for position ahead of looming competition in telecoms markets.

C&W confirmed that it was abandoning its German partnership called Vebacom, but Britain's second-biggest telecoms group denied that it was effectively pulling out of Europe, although it did not expects an imminent link-up with a global alliance.

C&W has been tipped as the "perfect partner" for Global One, a marriage between Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom and America's Sprint, because it has access to two key markets Global One lacks -- Britain and Asia.
But C&W, whose chief executive Richard Brown is a former Sprint executive, said a deal with Global One or any other such alliance looked some way off.
"We shall only do so if, after careful consideration, we are certain that it will add shareholder value," a spokeswoman said. "In any event, don't expect anything to happen quickly."

But while Veba had favoured attacking the German telecoms market with costly infrastructure investments, C&W wanted to concentrate on developing its Cable & Wireless Communications business. The unit was created after the merger of its British Mercury division with three other cable TV companies.
C&W's move to drop its German deal emphasises the high-risk nature of the vast investment telecoms groups need to free them from leasing phone lines from incumbent phone giants.

C&W said it had agreed to sell its 45 percent interest in the Vebacom GmbH mobile, cable and networks venture for 2.21 billion marks ($1.34 billion) and predicted a one-off pretax profit boost of 60 million pounds ($98.41 million) this year.
The sale, adjusted for its parallel 90 million mark buyout of Veba's half of the much smaller Cable & Wireless Europe, would lead to enhanced earnings in the year to March 31, 1998.
Veba has also pledged to remain a shareholder in C&W, hanging on to a 10.4 percent stake and removing the risk of a stock overhang depressing the British company's shares.
But some analysts said it was vital to distinguish between short-term presentational gains and long-term strategic issues.

C&W's remaining European operations are relatively small. Cable and Wireless Europe, which has operations in eight European countries, accrued losses of 16 million pounds in the six months to September 30, 1996.

The move marks the latest shift in the balance of power as phone groups jockey for position ahead of competition in European markets from 1998. Some telephone prices are already falling and some analysts fear margins will follow.

C&W's departure could weaken Vebacom, which hopes to become a serious challenger to Germany's telecoms giant Deutsche Telekom. And it might boost the competitive position of C&W's arch-rival, British Telecommunications

BT has linked up with German conglomerate Viag in a joint venture called Viag Interkom. That alliance, which hopes to become the second operator in Europe's richest telecoms market, was further strengthened on Thursday by recruiting Telenor, the Norwegian state-owned telecoms operator.
While Veba and its remaining German partner RWE said in Germany they were seeking a new international partner, some analysts have speculated they may link up with Viag Interkom.
RWE left Interkom to join Veba and C&W only last year. ($1=.6097 Pound) ($1=1.6506 Mark)
